column2: On the authority of Muʿādh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I said: “O Messenger of Allah,
tell me of a deed that will admit me to Paradise and keep me far from the Fire.” He said: “You have asked about something great, yet it is easy for the one for whom Allah the Exalted makes it easy:
worship Allah without associating anything with Him, establish the prayer, give the zakāh, fast Ramaḍān and make pilgrimage to the House.” Then he said: “Shall I not guide you to the gates of good?

Fasting is a shield; charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire; and a man's prayer in the depth of the night.” Then he recited: “Their sides forsake their beds…” until he reached “…they used to do” [al-Sajdah 32:16–17]. Then he said: “Shall I not tell you of the head of the matter, its pillar and its highest peak?”
I said: “Yes indeed, O Messenger of Allah.”
He said: “The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is the prayer, and its highest peak is jihād.” Then he said: “Shall I not tell you of what holds all of that together?”
I said: “Yes indeed, O Messenger of Allah.”
He took hold of his tongue and said: “Restrain this.” I said: “O Prophet of Allah,
will we really be taken to account for what we say?”
He said: “May your mother be bereaved of you!
Is there anything that topples people into the Fire on their faces”—or he said: “on their noses—except the harvests of their tongues?”
Reported by al-Tirmidhī, who said: “A ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ hadith.”
The verse quoted ends يعملون (“they used to do”, al-Sajdah 32:17); the edition prints يعلمون here and in commentary 4. The translation follows the Qurʾānic text.
His words, “I said: O Messenger of Allah,

tell me of a deed that will admit me to Paradise and keep me far from the Fire”, show the Companions' eagerness for good and for knowing the deeds by which Paradise is attained and safety from the Fire is secured. They also show that Paradise and the Fire exist,

and that the allies of Allah do righteous deeds in order to win Paradise and be safe from the Fire. This is contrary to what some Sufis say, that they do not worship Allah out of desire for His Paradise or fear of His Fire. That claim is false,
as the Companions' eagerness to know the deeds that lead to Paradise and keep one far from the Fire shows; and Allah tells us that His intimate friend [Ibrāhīm] said:

“And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss” [al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:85]. The hadith also shows that righteous deeds are a cause of entering Paradise. Many verses say so, among them the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: “And that is Paradise, which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do” [al-Zukhruf 43:72], and:

“Indeed, those who say ‘Our Lord is Allah’ and then remain upright—there will be no fear upon them, nor will they grieve. Those are the people of Paradise, abiding in it forever, as a reward for what they used to do” [al-Aḥqāf 46:13–14].
This does not contradict what is reported in the hadith: “None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds.” They said: “Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?”

He said: “Not even I, unless Allah envelops me in His mercy.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (6463) and Muslim (2816). The bāʾ (“by”) in the hadith denotes exchange, while in the verses it denotes causation: entering Paradise is not a price paid for deeds;

rather, righteous deeds are causes of it. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in His grace grants success in the cause, which is righteous deeds, and in His grace grants the reward, which is entering Paradise; so the grace, in both the cause and what it brings about, belongs to Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He.

His words, “You have asked about something great, yet it is easy for the one for whom Allah the Exalted makes it easy”, show the great standing and importance of this question and encourage asking such questions,
since the Messenger ﷺ described what was asked about as great.

Despite its greatness and the difficulty of doing it, the Prophet ﷺ followed this with what shows that it is easy and simple for the one for whom Allah makes it easy. This shows that the Muslim should be patient in acts of obedience even if they are hard on the soul,

because the outcome of patience is praiseworthy. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “And whoever fears Allah, He will make his matter easy for him” [al-Ṭalāq 65:4]; and he ﷺ said: “Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (6487) and Muslim (2822).
His words, “worship Allah without associating anything with Him, establish the prayer, give the zakāh, fast Ramaḍān and make pilgrimage to the House”:

the Prophet ﷺ made clear that the most important thing by which one draws near to Allah and wins Paradise and safety from the Fire is performing the obligations, which in this hadith are the five pillars of Islam mentioned in the hadith of Jibrīl and the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar,
“Islam is built upon five”. In the ḥadīth qudsī it is reported: “My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory on him.” His words,

“worship Allah without associating anything with Him”, set out the right of Allah, which is devoting worship sincerely to Allah; and included in it is the testimony that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah,
because the worship of Allah can be known only through believing him ﷺ and acting on what he brought.
Every deed by which one seeks nearness to Allah benefits its doer only if it is done sincerely for Allah and built on following the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
The two testimonies are inseparable: the testimony that there is no god but Allah must be accompanied by the testimony that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
These pillars are mentioned in the hadith in order of their importance. Prayer is put first because it is a firm bond between the servant and his Lord,
being repeated five times in a day and night. After it zakāh is mentioned,
because it comes only once a year and its benefit reaches both the one who pays it and the one who receives it; then after that fasting,
because it is repeated every year; and after it Ḥajj,
because it is obligatory only once in a lifetime.
His words, “Shall I not guide you to the gates of good?
Fasting is a shield; charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire; and a man's prayer in the depth of the night.” Then he recited: “Their sides forsake their beds…”

until he reached “…they used to do”: having made clear the obligations that are the cause of entering Paradise and being safe from the Fire, he ﷺ pointed the way to a number of voluntary deeds by which the Muslim gains an increase in faith, an increase in reward and the expiation of sins,

namely charity, fasting and the night prayer. He said of fasting, “Fasting is a shield (junnah)”; junnah means protection, and fasting is a protection in this world and the Hereafter. In this world it is a protection from falling into sins:
ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “O young men,
whoever of you is able to marry, let him marry, for it is more effective in lowering the gaze and guarding chastity; and whoever is not able, let him fast,

for it will be a restraint for him.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (1905) and Muslim (1400). In the Hereafter it is a protection from entering the Fire, as is reported in the hadith: “Whoever fasts a day in the path of Allah, Allah will keep his face seventy years' distance from the Fire.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (2840).

His words, “charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire”, show the great importance of voluntary charity, and that Allah the Exalted removes sins by it and extinguishes them as water extinguishes fire.

The sins meant are minor sins, and also major sins when one repents of them. The Prophet ﷺ likened charity's extinguishing of sins to water's extinguishing of fire, and this shows that the sins disappear entirely,
for what is observed when water falls on fire is that it removes it until nothing of it remains.

His words, “and a man's prayer in the depth of the night”: this is the third of the gates of good by which one draws near to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. At this point the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited the words of the Exalted:

“Their sides forsake their beds, calling upon their Lord in fear and hope, and they spend from what We have provided them. No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes as a reward for what they used to do” [al-Sajdah 32:16–17].
The Prophet ﷺ informed us that the best prayer after the obligatory prayer is the night prayer (reported by Muslim, 1163).
The Prophet ﷺ prepared the way for explaining these gates of good with a question, in his words to Muʿādh: “Shall I not guide you to the gates of good?”,
because that draws Muʿādh's attention to the importance of what was about to be imparted to him, so that he would prepare himself and be ready to take in all that was imparted to him.
His words, “Shall I not tell you of the head of the matter, its pillar and its highest peak?
I said: Yes indeed, O Messenger of Allah.

He said: The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is the prayer, and its highest peak is jihād”: what is meant by “the matter” is the affair that is the greatest of all affairs, namely the religion with which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent. Its head is Islam, which is general, including the prayer, jihād and other things.

He mentioned the prayer and described it as the pillar of Islam, likening it to a building that stands on its pillars; it is the most important of the bodily acts of worship whose benefit is limited to the one who does it.
Then he mentioned jihād, which includes striving against the self and striving against the enemies, both disbelievers and hypocrites, and described it as the highest peak of Islam,
because in jihād lies the strength of the Muslims and the prevailing of their religion and its ascendancy over other religions.
His words, “Shall I not tell you of what holds all of that together?
I said: Yes indeed, O Messenger of Allah.
He took hold of his tongue and said: Restrain this. I said: O Prophet of Allah,
will we really be taken to account for what we say?
He said: May your mother be bereaved of you!
Is there anything that topples people into the Fire on their faces—or he said: on their noses—except the harvests of their tongues?!
”: this shows the danger of the tongue: it is what plunges one into ruin, and what holds all good together lies in guarding it, so that nothing comes from it except what is good,
as he ﷺ said: “Whoever guarantees me what is between his jaws and what is between his legs, I guarantee him Paradise.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (6474). And he ﷺ said:
“Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent.” Ibn Rajab said in explaining this hadith in Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam (2/146–147):

“This shows that restraining, controlling and confining the tongue is the root of all good, and that whoever controls his tongue has controlled his affairs, mastered them and kept them in order.” He also said: “What is meant by the harvests of the tongues is the recompense and punishments of unlawful speech,
for a person sows good and bad deeds by his words and actions, and then on the Day of Resurrection he reaps what he sowed. Whoever sows good, in word or deed, reaps honour;

and whoever sows evil, in word or deed, will reap regret tomorrow. The apparent meaning of the hadith of Muʿādh shows that most of what people enter the Fire for is what they utter with their tongues; for the sin of speech includes shirk,

which is the greatest of sins with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; it includes speaking about Allah without knowledge, which is the companion of shirk; it includes false testimony, which has been equated with associating partners with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic;

and it includes sorcery, slander and other major and minor sins, such as lying, backbiting and talebearing. The other sins, those committed by action, are seldom free of words that accompany them and help to bring them about.”

His words, “May your mother be bereaved of you (thakilatka ummuka)”: Shaykh Ibn ʿUthaymīn said in his explanation of this hadith: “That is, may she lose you, so that she is bereaved by losing you. This sentence is not meant in its literal sense; it is meant only to urge and spur one to understand what is being said.”

In fact, such expressions, in this hadith and others like it, are a kind of supplication for the person addressed. Evidence of this is the hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (2603) from Anas, in which the Messenger ﷺ said: “O Umm Sulaym,
do you not know of the condition I made with my Lord? I stipulated with my Lord, saying: I am only a human being; I am pleased as humans are pleased and I become angry as humans become angry;

so whichever one of my nation I supplicate against with a supplication he does not deserve, [I asked] that He make it for him a purification, a cleansing and a means of nearness by which He brings him near to Himself on the Day of Resurrection.”

It is part of the precision of Imam Muslim (may Allah have mercy on him) and the excellent arrangement of his Ṣaḥīḥ that he placed after this hadith the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) about the Prophet's words concerning Muʿāwiyah, “May Allah not fill his stomach”, so that it is understood as a supplication for him, not against him.
The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) were eager for good and for knowing what leads to Paradise and keeps one far from the Fire.
Paradise and the Fire exist, and they are everlasting and will not perish.

One may worship Allah in the hope of entering Paradise and being safe from the Fire; it is not as some Sufis say, that Allah is not to be worshipped out of desire for His Paradise or fear of His Fire.
The deed asked about is important; indeed, it is great.
The path that leads to salvation is hard, and one can follow it only when Allah makes it easy.
The most important thing with which the two races [humans and jinn] have been charged is the worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; the books were sent down and the messengers sent for that.

The worship of Allah counts only if it is built on the two testimonies, which are inseparable, and no deed is accepted unless it is done sincerely for Allah and in conformity with what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ brought.
The pillars of Islam are of great importance,
since the Prophet ﷺ directed Muʿādh to them from among all the obligations Allah has prescribed.
These obligations are ranked in importance according to their order in this hadith.
Muslims are encouraged to do voluntary deeds along with the obligatory ones.
Among the most important things by which one draws near to Allah after performing the obligations are charity, fasting and the night prayer.
The prayer is of great importance: it is the pillar of Islam.
The hadith shows the merit of jihād: it is the highest peak of Islam.
The tongue is dangerous: it leads to ruin and plunges one into the Fire.
